new_statements.quote: Megjegyezzük végűl, hogy a vogulban általában a szó első tagjára esik a főhangsúly s a harmadikra a mellékhangsúly. […] Ez általános hangsúly-törvénytől csak a tavdai nyelv tér el sok tekintetben, ezért ebben a hangsúlyt minden egyes szón külön jelzem. || [a tatárok] nagy társadalmi hatása a vogulokra mutatkozik ezek nyelvének nemcsak szókincsében, mely telve van tatár elemekkel, hanem grammatikai részletekben is, minő pl. a hangsúly, melynek eredeti ugor természete egészen megváltozott. || A fölszólító mód második személyű alakjai egytagú töveknél a hangsuly tekintetében is külömböznek az egyes és többes számban, pl. äl- ölni: imp. sing. älén, plur äli'n!
new_statements.translation: We note finally that in Vogul the main stress generally falls on the first syllable of the word and the secondary stress on the third. […] Only the Tavda language deviates from this general stress law, in many respects, which is why in it I mark the stress separately on every single word. || [The Tatars'] great social influence on the Voguls shows in their language not only in the vocabulary, which is full of Tatar elements, but also in grammatical details, such as the stress, whose original Ugric nature has completely changed. || In the second-person imperative forms of monosyllabic stems, singular and plural differ also with respect to stress, e.g. äl- 'kill': imp. sing. älén, plur. älín!

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages are on the saved open scans. (1) NyK 21: 325-326, PDF pp. 343-344; page images /; extracted text): "Megjegyezzük végűl, hogy a vogulban általában a szó első tagjára esik a főhangsúly s a harmadikra a mellékhangsúly. Ép úgy mint a magyarban az igekötő elenyészteti az alapszó hangsúlyát.. Ez általános hangsúly-törvénytől csak a tavdai nyelv tér el sok tekintetben, ezért ebben a hangsúlyt minden egyes szón külön jelzem." Verbatim (scanned file has "végűi"/"mellókhangsúly"; the page image reads as quoted). (2) NyK 24: 152-153 (PDF p. 159; the text layer): "..tatárok letelepedése e vidéken, kiknek nagy társadalmi hatása a vogulokra mutatkozik ezek nyelvének nemcsak szók…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tavda Mansi is the one Mansi variety without initial stress. First-hand: Munkácsi (the only grammarian to hear it) says it departs from the general Mansi law (main stress on syllable 1, secondary on syllable 3) 'in many respects', attributes the change to Tatar influence, marks stress word by word, and shows it is contrastive (imp. sg. älén vs pl. älín); his own summary, quoted verbatim by Wichmann 1894: XIII from Munkácsi's German report (Ung. Rev. 1890: 590), is that the accent is variable and 'may fall on the last and the penultimate syllable of the word' (in disyllables = second syllable; his paradigms mark e.g. öránt 'waits', minánt 'goes', souránten 'you cut'). Kannisto 1919 marks accent only when it is not on syllable 1 and reports in TJ/TČ the reduction and even loss of the unstressed first-syllable vowel (p. 54). The modern synthesis is Honti 1975: 15 (Google-Books snippet, and as reported by Normanskaja 2020: 138): in di- and polysyllabic words the accent 'usually lies on the second syllable' in both nouns and verbs, so he does not mark it; Keresztes 1998 (snippet) and Szinnyei 1910: 52 give the same picture (second / 'mostly last or penultimate' syllable, apparently Tatar influence). Reading therefore: stress predominantly on the second syllable, i.e. non-initial and fixed for the bulk of the lexicon, with a residue of first-syllable-stressed words and forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Munkácsi's general Mansi law puts a secondary stress on the third syllable, but he says Tavda departs from the law and gives no Tavda secondary-stress rule; no other source mentions secondary stress for Tavda.
new_statements.exceptions: Munkácsi 1894: 327: imperative 2nd person distinguished by stress alone in monosyllabic and j-final stems (sing. älén / plur. älín; jäjin 'come!' vs jäjín 'come (pl.)!'); phrasal shift 'teu jant, íntém äk?' (p. 325); many paradigm forms left unmarked (= initial stress). Normanskaja 2020: 136-139 finds in Munkácsi's and Kannisto's Tavda material two/three accent paradigms (some verbs fixed on the root, others fixed on the second syllable, some Tavda texts of Kannisto never initial, others mixed) and rejects the 'always second syllable' generalization of Steinitz 1955 / Kannisto 2013; Honti 1975 himself hedges with 'gewöhnlich' and notes the collectors marked accent inconsistently. Polysyllables: Munkácsi/Szinnyei say last or penultimate, Honti says second.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation and paradigm forms as transcribed in 1888-89 (Munkácsi) and 1901-06 (Kannisto); the first-hand quote establishes non-initial, contrastive, mobile stress but does not itself name the syllable — the 'second syllable' rule is Honti 1975: 15 (snippet-only here, reported by Normanskaja 2020) and Keresztes 1998 (snippet-only). Wichmann's 1894 verbatim quotation of Munkácsi ('letzte und vorletzte wortsilbe') is in a saved open file (MSFOu 7: XIII) but is second-hand transmission of Munkácsi's Ungarische Revue 1890 report.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sout3253 = the Tavda (Tawda) dialect group, the only Southern Mansi variety ever recorded. All first-hand data come from two fieldworkers: Munkácsi 1888-89 (villages Čandyri = 'felső tavdai' FT and Košuki = 'alsó tavdai' AT, Košuki volost) and Kannisto 1901-06 (Janyčkova TJ, Čandyri TČ, Gorodok TG). Honti 1975 (and Normanskaja 2020) analyse Kannisto's TJ/TČ material; Munkácsi's stress marks are the basis of Wichmann 1894 and Szinnyei 1910. The dialect was extinct by the 1960s (Rombandeeva 2017: one semi-speaker found in 1963), so no instrumental or modern description can exist.

sources.note: p. 325-326: in Vogul generally main stress on the first syllable, secondary on the third; preverbs and negative particles absorb the stress of the following word; 'only the Tavda language deviates from this general stress law in many respects, therefore in it I mark the stress separately on every word'.

sources.note: p. 136-139, 141-145: reports that in Kannisto's dictionary (2013) 'in two-syllable words or bases, the stress in Tavda dialect always falls on the second syllable, both in verbs and in nouns. This fact is noted in L. Honti's monograph (1975 : 15)'; Steinitz 1955: 331-336 says Kannisto 'in the southern dialects noted the accent always on the second syllable'; her own reading of Munkácsi 1894: 289 and Kannisto-Liimola 1951 texts: Tavda has accent paradigms I (fixed on root) and II (fixed on second syllable), some texts never initial, others mixed.
